stories.headline: Wizards' AJ Dybantsa (ankle) to miss season opener
stories.summary: AJ Dybantsa, the No. 1 pick in the NBA draft, will miss the Wizards' season opener Wednesday because of an ankle injury.
stories.body:
The Washington Wizards will have to wait a little longer before seeing the regular-season debut of their No. 1 pick.

AJ Dybantsa will miss the team's Wednesday night season opener against the Milwaukee Bucks with an ankle injury, coach Brian Keefe announced Tuesday.

Dybantsa will be day-to-day with the injury he suffered in Friday's preseason finale. Keefe termed the injury a mild ankle sprain Friday.

Dybantsa fell to the ground after landing awkwardly on his left ankle following a midrange jump shot before limping to the locker room. He had scored 12 points in 15 minutes before his exit in the second quarter.

The next chance for Dybantsa to make his debut would be Friday night at home against the Toronto Raptors before the team plays at Chicago on Saturday in the first of three straight road games.

stories.headline: Panthers' Brady Tkachuk to donate Senators jerseys thrown in protest
stories.summary: Brady Tkachuk, who was traded from Ottawa to Florida in June, says he'll donate any Senators jerseys thrown in protest of his return to to the Boys and Girls Club of Ottawa.
stories.body:
Brady Tkachuk expects an unruly reception as he returns to Ottawa for the first time on Wednesday, after the Senators traded him to the Florida Panthers in the offseason. But if any of his No. 7 Ottawa jerseys hit the ice in protest, Tkachuk has plans to use them for a good cause.

On his "Wingmen" podcast on Tuesday, Tkachuk said he spoke with the Panthers and "every jersey that gets thrown on the ice is going to get donated to the Boys and Girls Club of Ottawa."

While Tkachuk said he doesn't "recommend doing it," but does anticipate he might see some fans toss their jerseys on the ice in protest.

Tkachuk was traded in June after having told Senators management that he didn't intend to sign an extension when his contract is up in 2028. He used his no-movement clause to force a trade to the Panthers, joining his brother and podcast co-host Matthew Tkachuk in South Florida.

"Clearly, it was pointed at one team at the end," said Ottawa GM Steve Staios.

Tkachuk's departure was contentious among Ottawa fans, saying he was "fully committed" to the franchise back in April. His return to face the Senators on Wednesday will be the first chance for those fans to let their displeasure known.

"If you're going to do it and send a message, just know that it's going to a good cause. I've received your message," said Tkachuk.

Matthew Tkachuk said he would like to see "10,000 Tkachuk jerseys on the ice" on Wednesday night.

Brady Tkachuk said the Boys and Girls Club is a "special place" where he and his wife Emma forged many meaningful relationships during their time in Ottawa.

Tkachuk played 572 games over 8 seasons with the Senators, who drafted him 4th overall in the 2018 NHL Draft. He scored 213 goals with 250 assists, as well as 821 penalty minutes as a physical tone-setter for the team. He served as team captain for five seasons, succeeding Erik Karlsson.

"This is the game that's been circled. I'm going to assume I'm not the only one that's had it circled," he said. "The place is still special to me. Eight years. I've experienced so much. Became a father and a husband during my time there. They have such amazing people that makes that organization tick and I'm excited to see them."

Tkachuk said he expected to have dinner with some former Ottawa teammates on Tuesday night, organized by defenseman and Olympic gold medal teammate Jake Sanderson.

stories.headline: Cesc Fàbregas calls suggestions he could replace Michael Carrick at Man United disrespectful
stories.summary: Cesc Fabregas has dismissed suggestions he could be in line to replace Michael Carrick as disrespectful.
stories.body:
COMO, Italy -- Cesc Fàbregas has dismissed suggestions he could be in line to replace Michael Carrick as disrespectful.

Fàbregas and Carrick will go head to head on Wednesday when Como face Manchester United in the Champions League.

The former Chelsea, Arsenal and Barcelona midfielder was asked at his pre-match news conference about the possibility of taking over from Carrick, who is under pressure following a run of six games without a win.

But Fàbregas refused to answer and hit back at the line of enquiry.

"I won't answer that question because I think that's not a very nice question," Fàbregas said on Tuesday.

"I don't think that shows enough respect to a great footballer and manager like Michael Carrick at the helm of a wonderful Manchester United side."

United travel to Italy with just two wins all season and without a victory in any competition for more than a month.

Como, meanwhile, are fifth in the Serie A table and warmed up for United's visit with a 3-1 win over Fiorentina on Sunday.

- Erik ten Hag: Cristiano Ronaldo 'let the team down' at Man United

"Manchester United is a historical club I know very, very well," said Fàbregas.

"We have so much respect for who they are, for what they do, because they have incredible players.

"I know Steve Holland very well because I worked with him for years at Chelsea and I know Michael has done really well in previous clubs as well.

"Last year he did really well bringing Manchester United back to where they belong, which is the Champions League, for the first time in many years, so it's not all bad. It's an honour to host them for the first time in our history."

stories.headline: How Rays' unique approach carried Tampa Bay to World Series
stories.summary: The small-market Rays are kings of the American League. Here's what Tampa Bay does that nobody else can match.
stories.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida -- Self-awareness is the Tampa Bay Rays' superpower. A natural disaster tore the roof off their home, and their franchise player torpedoed his career in the ugliest manner imaginable, and never did the Rays fall prey to doubt. Baseball can be brutal and unrelenting and unforgiving, but when the world seemed to conspire against them, the Rays found solace in the one thing in which they never stopped believing: themselves.

Their trip to the 122nd World Series, booked with a rollicking 7-3 victory against the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night, crystallized the power of Tampa Bay's method and delivered madness to the 40,230 who filled Tropicana Field. Over the past two decades, the Rays had built something meaningful. Competing in a comically moneyed AL East, habitually dispossessed by comparison, the Rays leaned on that acute understanding of exactly who they are -- an organization that deifies a culture of questioning, improvement and accountability -- as their great equalizer. They stuck to these principles even after the demise of the career of Wander Franco, around whom they planned to build their franchise, and when damage to the Trop from Hurricane Milton forced them to a temporary home for the 2025 season.

And so through it all, the Rays did what the Rays always do, which is rely on a process honed through years of commitment to a single purpose: winning -- regardless of the impediments that exist.

"We have people that truly care about what they do," Rays president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. "Staff and players alike with a prevailing belief that we can win a championship here. A relentless pursuit of improvement by way of respecting all our differences and finding the good in each and everybody involved in this organization."

Neander leads a baseball operations department nearly 200 heads deep, and from it was born this group of 26, many of them misfit toys. Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz, acquired in separate trades with the Guardians three years apart, supplied a pair of late-inning two-run home runs that provided the margin of victory. Freddy Peralta, secured in a deadline deal with the New York Mets in August, contributed 5 1⁄3 innings of high-octane pitching en route to ALCS MVP honors. Fifty-four innings of error-free baseball in the series reinforced that the Rays did not win the most games in the league by accident. They know who they are, and they spend every day seeking validation not for that but rather for what it breeds.

Which is a brand of baseball strikingly similar to that of their World Series opponent, the Milwaukee Brewers, the best team in the National League. The Rays and Brewers are baseball Rorschach tests. Some see them through the lens of their payrolls, 26th and 19th, respectively, and the size of their markets, 19th and 30th. That's too simple, though. The Rays and Brewers are not what they spend; they are what they produce, and that happens to be wondrous displays of baseball, from their multidimensional offensive approaches to their parade of arms that propel baseballs in manners that stretch the limits of the human body to the pride they take in minutiae, from defense to bunting to base stealing.

This World Series, in other words, is no accident, not some stroke of luck that will be painted as a battle of unlikelies. Doing so is a disservice to everything the Rays and Brewers are, which is proof that the power of money -- and suggesting it isn't an inherent advantage would be disingenuous-- has its limits. Namely, organizations that actively commingle the old and new, whether it's scouting and statistics or small ball and big flies. Without that ethos -- and without the certitude that it's right -- Caminero would not have been dancing on the field Monday night, holding a flag declaring the Rays AL champions.

It was not the first time Caminero inspired the Trop to ear-splitting decibels Monday, urged on by what was unfolding on the field. Up in the seventh inning against the Guardians' impermeable closer, Cade Smith, Caminero saw a split-fingered fastball boring inside and unfurled the fastest swing in the major leagues. Smith had thrown 884 splitters in his big league career without yielding a home run, only to see the 885th clang off the left-field foul pole.

Caminero went into showman mode, turning to his teammates and pounding his chest before touching first base. Nearly 40 seconds after his home run trot began, Caminero finished it by stopping a stride shy of home plate, turning toward the stands, pointing to one specific person and crossing his arms, full boss-mode.

He was looking at Randy Arozarena, the former Rays outfielder who hit a record 10 postseason home runs the last time Tampa Bay advanced to the World Series in 2020 and punctuated his best moments with that signature pose. Though he'd since been traded to Seattle, Arozarena wasn't going to miss this game, nor was Tyler Glasnow, the former Rays pitcher who had left in a deal to the Los Angeles Dodgers, winners of the past two World Series.

Once a Ray, always a Ray isn't some platitude. It is, perhaps, the foremost explanation of who they are and why they find themselves four wins from the first championship in franchise history.

Before the ninth inning of Game 6 began, Shane McClanahan found Yandy Díaz in the dugout and told him exactly where Díaz was going to hit a home run. The two are the most tenured members of the Rays, and even if dugout home run predictions are notoriously wrong, McClanahan felt something coming, a function of spending the last six seasons studying Díaz's consistent excellence.

"From Day 1, we've instilled it in every single person in this clubhouse," said McClanahan, who started the 2022 All-Star Game but is out for the postseason with left forearm tightness. "We're a team-first group. We're no egos. We play for each other, and we play hard. That's why he gave me that bear hug in the dugout at the end. I called the shot, man."

Losing a trade is painful enough -- and the Guardians unequivocally lost both deals with Tampa Bay. Caminero has turned from a rookie-ball flier into an MVP candidate. Díaz has posted the 10th-best on-base percentage in baseball since joining Tampa Bay in 2019. Losing a season to those who left in trades, as Cleveland just did, is insult, injury and indignity. And yet Caminero and Díaz comprise less than 8% of the Tampa Bay roster Neander and his band of dreamers constructed, so often via trades and unexpected signings.

Take Nick Martinez. Three days before spring training, the 36-year-old right-hander was unemployed. Tampa Bay, looking to expand its pitching depth, considered the array of available talent: future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander, veteran Chris Bassitt and right-hander Zack Littell, who, like many that go to the Rays, had demonstrably improved in his time there the prior two-plus seasons before being traded to Cincinnati at the 2025 deadline. When Neander reiterated the primary intention of any pitching signing -- "We are going to prioritize the one that's going to leave a lasting impression on their teammates," he told his group -- they kept gravitating back to Martinez.

He was, it turned out, an archetypal Ray despite never having worn navy and Columbia blue. Up at 23. Out of the league four years later and off to the Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters. Resurrected by four years in Japan before a return to the United States led to four solid seasons split between San Diego and Cincinnati. Because Martinez's fastball rarely exceeds 93 mph, teams let him rot in free agency until the Rays gave him a one-year, $13 million contract.

Their read on Martinez proved fortuitous. Pitchers gravitated toward him, as did hitters -- rare for clubhouses traditionally bifurcated by position. He spoke English and Spanish. He had lived a rich baseball life, full enough to serve as the glue that kept the Rays together, whether it was at a cigar bar or on a golf course or at copious team dinners that drew more than 20 teammates without fail.

"These guys make it easy, really," Martinez said. "They wanna hang. I can throw team dinners every week, and if no one shows up, no one shows up. These guys showed up. Camaraderie matters. It's a big part of our formula. The more you hang out with someone, the more you get to know someone. The more you get to know someone, the more you root for that person. We played for each other the whole season. We have no egos here. We just wanna do what the game asks of us and play for each other and celebrate together. We play very selfless baseball."

That manifested itself early. On April 18, the Rays faced Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes and looked helpless through four scoreless innings. A rain delay of nearly 2½ hours followed, chasing Skenes and allowing Tampa Bay to chip away before winning 8-7 in 13 innings. In the aftermath of a long and perilous day, they stuck around in the clubhouse postgame, slugging beers, talking ball, a recurring theme throughout the season. The work of winning inside the white lines begins outside of them.

"This organization has a wonderful reputation of knowing how to win, how to get the best out of their guys," Martinez said. "They communicate the best I've ever been around. Tampa's always been on the list for me to come play for, and when they came calling, man, we ran with it."

By June 27, they captured a spot atop the AL East that they would not relinquish on their march to 98 wins. New heroes emerged daily. Cam Booser didn't even join the team until June and wound up one of the best relief pitchers in baseball and the personification of Tampa Bay's ability to help rescue what once was lost.

After five injury-riddled seasons in which he didn't advance past High-A, Booser retired in 2017 and went to work in construction. Four years later, when coaching kids in Washington, Booser realized he was still throwing in the high 90s from the left side and joined the independent Chicago Dogs, where he was scouted by Rays executive Kevin Ibach. While that gig didn't lead to a job in affiliated ball, Booser surfaced with the Boston Red Sox in 2024 and debuted at 32 years old before kicking around the last two years and finding a home in St. Petersburg.

"They make you feel special here, no matter who you are," Booser said. "They treat you all the same no matter who you are. If you're here, you're important. They take the time to invest in every single player, and they just believe in you. More than maybe you believe in yourself at the time. And that's infectious. They're consistent every single day. It's how they work. They trust the process no matter what, and you start to believe that."

Booser's belief came from the cluster of players he saw improving, compounded by the Rays' specific suggestions for his optimization. They wanted him to double down on the cutter he had thrown far less frequently the previous season. Booser knew Drew Rasmussen, the staff ace, and Griffin Jax, who arrived in a trade with Minnesota at the 2025 deadline. They couldn't say enough good things about the Rays.

"I understood they do things very differently here, in the best way possible," Booser said. "And I wanted to be a part of that."

He's not the only one. A common refrain throughout baseball is how many things the Rays do well, from scouting to drafting to international signing to player development. At the top of the list is taking an unlikely group and turning the players into productive big leaguers. Evaluators thought Jonathan Aranda was positionless with a bad body. He was an All-Star last year. Coming into this season, Ryan Vilade had played 28 big league games with four teams. The Rays recognized he crushed left-handed pitching and leaned on him in 96 games this year as a platoon specialist. The Guardians cast aside Richie Palacios after taking him in the third round of the 2018 MLB draft. He resurfaced with the Rays and batted .500 in the ALCS with a two-run double in Game 6 that staked the Rays a 2-0 advantage.

"They have a unique way of making guys feel very comfortable with who they are," said Rays shortstop Taylor Walls, who, despite poor offensive performance, maintains the starting job because the Rays so deeply value his defense. "When guys enter the organization, they can sense that people really have their back, that they can really be themselves and not be afraid to make mistakes, to really just be great at what they're great at and not try to do anything else outside of that. And I think it really allows guys to find out who they are, to give themselves an identity and just to buy in."

Buying in wasn't a problem for Peralta, who joined catcher Liam Hicks and Booser's co-setup man, Tyler Wells, as the Rays' deadline acquisitions. Peralta, 30, spent his first eight years with the Brewers until they dealt him to the New York Mets over the winter, one season before he was due to hit free agency. As the Mets crumbled, so did Peralta. After Tampa Bay snagged him at the deadline for three minor leaguers, coaches and other staff sat with him in Colorado and "were very clear with me. They told me, 'We know who you are. We know what you have done and your whole career. We're not looking at the last three months of your career. We know who you are, and we're gonna help you to get your confidence back.' And, you know, in the moment, I believed them."

The belief was warranted. The Rays wanted Peralta to throw his devastating changeup more often, and with it came an uptick in his fastball velocity. In his last six regular-season starts, he posted a 0.79 ERA in 34 innings. In 12 innings spread over two starts and one relief appearance in the ALCS, Peralta allowed one run, winning Games 2 and 6, capturing the hardware to match his NLCS MVP counterpart, Jake Bauers -- who the Rays traded in 2018 in a deal to get Díaz. Offering substantive advice, scraping for marginal value, endlessly trying to get better -- the Rays' way was familiar, and comfortable, to Peralta for good reason.

"It's very similar," he said, "to Milwaukee."

Self-awareness is not just about knowing what you are. It's recognizing what you aren't, and, in that respect, the Rays and Brewers are kindred spirits. The same inequities that limit the Rays constrain the Brewers, and it's what makes this World Series so tantalizing: The parties occupy similar ground.

The Brewers have not made the World Series in 44 years and have not captured a championship in their 58 years of existence. The Rays lost in both of their previous World Series appearances -- falling to Philadelphia in 2008 and Los Angeles in 2020 -- and are title-free for 29 seasons. There will be a first-time World Series winner this year, amplifying the stakes -- and the crowds at American Family Field, where Game 1 begins Friday with Brewers ace and soon-to-be NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski against Rasmussen.

For all of the narrative to come about the grand meaning of the Rays and Brewers facing barely a month before the league is set to lock out the players who won't agree to a salary cap the league has positioned as necessary to help small-market teams, this World Series is, as much as anything, a pure display of the game, a collision of the present with the past.

It already was evident with the Rays, even as they clinched. They wore Devil Rays jerseys, a vestige of their early years. The Caminero-Arozarena exchange was generational aura. Even the team's past leadership was present, with former team president Matt Silverman joining Patrick Zalupski, Bill Cosgrove and Ken Babby, the new ownership group that bought the team in September 2025 and intends to replace the aged Trop with a new stadium in Tampa.

The Rays' stability, in part, has come from their ability to complement their longtime employees with new faces to replace those who left the Tampa Bay machine and eventually took over other baseball operations departments: Andrew Friedman (Dodgers), Chaim Bloom (Boston and St. Louis), Peter Bendix (Miami), James Click (Houston), Taylor Smith (A's) and Matt Arnold, who runs the Brewers. The Rays' fingerprints are everywhere in baseball.

"Since I was drafted at 17, every coach that I've been with, the players they drafted, you could tell that everybody was just a straight-up A-plus human being," Walls said. "And if they weren't, they got out. You've got to be a good person to be in this organization. You gotta care about winning. Winning has to be your only priority. And if it's not, they sniff you out real quick and you're probably not here long."

Plenty do stay. Scout Mitch Lukevics joined the Rays three years before they debuted in 1998 and hasn't left. As teams across the industry have cut scouting jobs, Ibach has bulked up the Rays' department with trusted pro personnel specialists Mike Brown, Max Cohen, Jason Cole, Jaosn Grey, Nate Howard and Mike Langill. They're the rare big league organization featuring multiple women in high-ranking baseball-operations positions, with assistant GM Chanda Lawdermilk, director of position player programming Dani Dockx and director of baseball operations Sammi Bireley, who has been pulling double duty to graduate recently from law school. Jon Daniels, the general manager of two Texas Rangers World Series teams, found refuge with Tampa Bay. Super-scout Bobby Heck did the same after Houston whacked its scouting department. Jeff Sullivan, the longtime FanGraphs wordsmith, is eight years into a multipurpose role with the organization. The Rays this year hired three former big leaguers -- Mike Ford, Beau Sulser and Joe Hudson -- to seed the next generation of front office talent. The pipeline doesn't run dry because Neander and his other deputies, Hamilton Marx and Will Cousins, refuse to let it.

All of them, and plenty more, deserve to be named because, as Booser said, "all our success is just a credit to our front office." And to Kevin Cash, the manager who guides the fruits of that labor with pitching coach Kyle Snyder and hitting coach Chad Mottola. They are the ticking heart of Tampa Bay's operation, the ones who made playing in a minor league park in 2025 palatable while the Trop was undergoing Extreme Makeover: Stadium Edition, the ones who have brought calm no matter the challenge.

Now Caminero and Diaz are swatting balls for the Rays instead of against them, Walls is picking balls no other shortstop would reach, and Chandler Simpson is burning around the basepaths faster than anyone in the big leagues. Rasmussen did snow angels in the confetti strewn about the Trop's turf after Hicks squeezed the final out of the ALCS, secured by All-Star closer Bryan Baker, who was acquired from Baltimore for the 37th overall draft pick in a 2025 trade. It was a proper celebration for a proper team that knows exactly what it is. How the rest of the world sees it will depend on the next 11 days, but after Monday, at least one thing is no longer in question: The Rays are, as they've been for most of the year, the class of the AL.

As for all of baseball, the 103-win Brewers might have something to say about that. They'll get a chance to on the field. The Rays' self-awareness extends to the World Series, and they understand just how good their opponent is, but that doesn't disabuse them of a core tenet that won't go away anytime soon.

They believe.

stories.headline: Christian Horner opposed Liam Lawson's short-lived Red Bull move: 'Shouldn't have been promoted'
stories.summary: Christian Horner has opened up on his reservations about Liam Lawson's short-lived Red Bull tenure in 2025, claiming the New Zealander "really shouldn't have been promoted in the first place."
stories.body:
Christian Horner has opened up on his reservations about Liam Lawson's short-lived Red Bull tenure in 2025, claiming the New Zealander "really shouldn't have been promoted in the first place."

The inexperienced Lawson was surprisingly picked to replace Sergio Pérez as Max Verstappen's new teammate in December 2024, but former team boss Horner says in his new autobiography, Drive, that he was uneasy with the decision and that it was Red Bull adviser Helmut Marko who pushed for the promotion.

Lawson was dropped after only two races, before Red Bull swiftly turned to Yuki Tsunoda.

"Liam was another racer from the junior programme and Helmut had championed the promotion, but I felt uncomfortable," Horner wrote.

"He was young and inexperienced, with only eleven Formula One races to his name, and we would be asking a huge amount from him."

Horner also accused Marko of playing political games over the decision, claiming the Austrian had told Lawson he was responsible for securing the drive.

"Meanwhile, Helmut was playing games," Horner wrote. "Before the final race of the season in Abu Dhabi, he had informed Liam that he would be driving for Red Bull because of his influence.

"When I challenged Helmut on this, he typically denied everything."

Lawson was promoted following Pérez's difficult 2024 campaign, which saw Red Bull finish third in the constructors' championship despite Verstappen winning his fourth consecutive drivers' title.

The New Zealander had impressed during two spells with the team's junior outfit but struggled immediately after stepping up to Red Bull.

He qualified 18th for the season-opening Australian Grand Prix before crashing out of the race, and then qualified last for both the sprint and the race in China.

"Liam only lasted two races," Horner wrote. "He struggled in pre-season testing and was clearly uncomfortable with the RB21's difficult handling characteristics.

"His confidence was smashed and, as with Pierre Gasly and Alex Albon, his arrival at Red Bull had come too soon.

"Sensing that the pressure on Liam was unfair, we replaced him."

- Horner: Red Bull blocked moves for Leclerc and Alonso

- Rafael Câmara to Haas: How he could shake up Ferrari's future

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title at the US Grand Prix

Horner said Honda, Red Bull's engine partner at the time, welcomed the decision to promote Japanese driver Tsunoda.

"The move back [to Racing] Bulls was tough for Liam," Horner wrote. "But he really shouldn't have been promoted in the first place."

Lawson returned to Racing Bulls, while Tsunoda remained alongside Verstappen for the rest of the 2025 season.

Horner was subsequently dismissed as Red Bull team principal and CEO in July 2025.

Lawson said earlier this year that Red Bull created a false narrative around the reasons behind his early exit from the team. The 24-year-old said he wasn't "mentally struggling" and that Red Bull had actually pushed him towards a "wild" setup change to find performance, which ultimately hampered his pace. He added that he now pretends in his mind he "never even went there."

Drive, Christian Horner's autobiography, will be released on Oct. 22.

stories.headline: Six players finally getting their time in the spotlight in the WNBA Finals
stories.summary: They might not have been instant stars in the WNBA, but these six players are having a huge impact on the Finals.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Kaila Charles got in position for her most important rebound of the season. Her Golden State Valkyries were clinging to a two-point lead in the closing seconds of Saturday's Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. The Dream had just launched a 3-pointer and Atlanta's Angel Reese, the league's top rebounder the past three years, was waiting for a potential tying putback.

But Charles boxed her out and grabbed the missed shot. That led to two free throws by Golden State teammate Gabby Williams to seal the series opener for the Valkyries. In all, Charles got three defensive rebounds in the final 1 minute, 7 seconds of a close, intense game.

"Kai is all about heart and hustle," Golden State coach Natalie Nakase said. "We've really been leaning on [her] in moments when she comes in. She changes the game."

Charles is one of several players making an impact in the Finals who might not have been instant stars when they arrived in the league but have found the right fit.

Others, such as Atlanta's Jordin Canada, have been successful in the past but have now fully stepped into the spotlight this postseason. In Monday's Game 2, Canada registered 13 points, 10 assists and seven rebounds to help the Dream even the series 1-1 with a 79-65 victory.

Here are six players having breakout moments who have shown that timing is everything.

Gabby Williams: 'Just go at me'

Williams maintains it's less about her blossoming and more about her not being given respect in the past. But statistically, her impact has never been bigger than right now, and her popularity is at its zenith with Valkyries fans. With Williams in her eighth WNBA season but her first in the Bay Area, Golden State has been the best fit for her in every aspect.

The Chicago Sky drafted Williams out of UConn with the No. 4 pick in 2018, and she played there three seasons. She was traded to the Los Angeles Sparks prior to the 2021 campaign, but she didn't play in the WNBA that year as she concentrated on competing in the Olympics with the French national team. Williams' time with Team France has helped expand her game and perhaps even more importantly has made her feel appreciated.

The Sparks traded Williams to the Storm before the 2022 season, and she was with Seattle through 2025, although she played just 10 games in 2023 and 12 in 2024. Then last season, she broke out with the Storm: Williams played all 44 games, made her first All-Star Game, was on the All-Defensive first team and averaged career highs in points, assists and steals.

After signing with Golden State this season, Williams improved her scoring average to a career-best 14.4 points and was again selected to the All-Defensive first team. Making her first appearance in the WNBA Finals, she led the Valkyries with 26 points in Game 1.

"Her 'killer' mode goes up a level every game," Nakase said. "The best thing she told me is, 'Just go at me. Like in games, I need directness.'

"Those are the best players to coach, because you can just say [something] right away and it doesn't waste time. The fact that she told me her coaching style right away made us grow closer together."

Jordin Canada: 'The most rewarding year'

Canada hasn't had to worry about having a WNBA job; she has started more than 70% of her games across a nine-year career. But she has never shined so brightly as she has in 2026, a culmination of her growth and resilience through injuries.

"She's just everything you'd want from a point guard," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Drafted No. 5 out of UCLA in 2018 by Seattle, she won two WNBA titles as a backup to Hall of Famer Sue Bird during four campaigns there.

"I'm a lot older now. I've learned a lot," Canada said of this Finals appearance. "Obviously, I'm in a different role than I was my first two championships of coming off the bench and trying to figure out where I can get in."

After two years with the Los Angeles Sparks, Canada was traded to Atlanta before the 2024 season. Injuries limited her to 20 games in 2024 and 28 in 2025. But she has played all but one game this year while averaging 31.1 minutes, during which she averaged 11.6 points and a career-best 7.3 assists in the regular season with those numbers increasing to 16.7 and 8.7 in the playoffs.

"My leadership has grown over the years, being able to talk more, communicate more, bring my championship experience to this team," Canada said. "Those are just some of the ways that I feel that I have grown. It's been the most rewarding year that I've had."

Veronica Burton: The 'smartest worker'

A three-time Big Ten defensive player of the year at Northwestern, Burton was the No. 7 pick in the 2022 draft and stayed with the Dallas Wings for two seasons. Cut just before the 2024 campaign, Burton was signed by the Connecticut Sun. But she was left available in the expansion draft, and Golden State took her. It has been the perfect fit.

"It's about understanding that when one door closes, that doesn't mean all of them are closed," Burton said of her WNBA path. "It may not go exactly as you initially imagined, but I hope people can learn from my journey."

Burton was the WNBA's Most Improved Player in 2025 and was on the All-Defensive Team this season and last. This year, she averaged a career-high 12.2 points in the regular season and ranked No. 9 in the WNBA in assists (5.7). While her averages have dropped in the playoffs, her impact has endured.

Nakase said that helping Burton reach her best these past two seasons is the same process she has used with other players.

"It's just asking them the questions ... what is your learning style and what do you need from me?" Nakase said. "She said, 'I just need someone to believe in me as a coach.'

"Her work ethic is the best. Last year, she showed up too much, like 8 in the morning. She learned to trust me that you don't always have to be the 'hardest' worker, you have to be the smartest worker."

Kiah Stokes: 'Clicked immediately'

The 6-foot-3 center has as much championship experience as anyone in this series, with three NCAA titles at UConn and three WNBA titles with the Las Vegas Aces. The No. 11 pick in the 2015 draft by the Liberty, Stokes spent five full seasons with New York. (She sat out in 2019.) Then in 2021, she was waived by the Liberty in late June after playing nine games.

Two days later, Las Vegas signed her -- and the best part of her pro career began. She won the 2022, 2023 and 2025 championships with the Aces. Stokes was a valuable part of the team but understandably was overshadowed by perennial league MVP A'ja Wilson.

Now with the Valkyries, Stokes is a full-time starter, averaging her most minutes (22.3) during the regular season since 2020 with New York. Her scoring (3.6) and rebounding (5.8) averages don't stand out, but the way she does everything the Valkyries need -- screening, passing, help defense, rim protection -- has in many ways made this her signature season.

Despite the Game 2 loss, Stokes on Monday joined Brittney Griner (2014) as the only players in WNBA history to record four-plus blocks in consecutive Finals games.

Her personality meshes with that of Nakase, who was an Aces assistant while Stokes was with Las Vegas.

"We clicked immediately," Stokes said. "We understand each other. She understands the game. She understands the work ethic."

Naz Hillmon: 'A reality check'

Hillmon was the program changer at Michigan, the most important recruit in coach Kim Barnes Arico's mission to make the Wolverines a contender. Hillmon led Michigan to its first Sweet 16 in 2021 and its first Elite Eight in 2022, after which she was a second-round pick by the Dream at No. 15. That was a steal for Atlanta: No player in that draft class has played more WNBA regular-season games (201) than Hillmon.

She was an elite scorer at 18.3 points per game over her college career. In the WNBA, she went to Atlanta along with the No. 1 pick in the same draft in Rhyne Howard, who has been one of the Dream's top scorers. Hillmon realized she needed to become a different type of player to excel in the WNBA. She focused more on defense, screening and facilitating. Then she dramatically improved her shooting range, going from just one made 3-pointer across her first three WNBA seasons to 53 in 2025 and 52 in 2026.

"It takes looking in the mirror and seeing that everybody can't be a star player once you get to this level," Hillmon said. "It's a reality check, but I feel I've always been someone who is selfless in doing whatever my team needs me to do. Being an undersized post player, how do I stay in this league as long as I possibly can?"

Hillmon was the WNBA's Sixth Player of the Year last season. She has started all but three of the Dream's games this year, averaging a career-best 9.1 points.

"She has really developed her game the last two years," Smesko said. "She's always been a good cutter and offensive rebounder and somebody who's willing to screen and get other people open. She has really found her rhythm and is also taking on the top defensive assignments."

Kaila Charles: 'Staying the course'

Charles started all 135 games she played at Maryland and was a three-time All-Big Ten first-team selection. But as a 6-foot-1 guard who made just 10 3-pointers in her college career, she fell to the next-to-last pick in the second round, No. 23, of the 2020 draft. However, only four of the 22 players taken ahead of her have played more than Charles' 135 WNBA regular-season games. Many are out of the league, but Charles persevered.

After her first two seasons with Connecticut and brief stints in Atlanta (one game in 2022) and Seattle (four games in 2023), she didn't play in the WNBA in 2024. In 2025, she joined Dallas but was released after 17 games.

Then Golden State called. She had three consecutive seven-day contracts before signing on for the rest of the 2025 campaign. She's now finishing the first season of a two-year deal with the Valkyries.

"I have been cut from multiple different teams, but one thing that never wavered was my belief that I belong," Charles said. "It was just finding a coach that believed in me, finding the right fit, and then just staying the course. I was playing overseas; I was playing here. I was staying ready for my moment."

Nakase praises the resilience of Charles, who represents a blue-collar determination Valkyries fans admire.

"The other day, I was at Safeway [grocery store], and someone gave me some flowers, a random lady," Charles said. "It was just really sweet. I really do feel the love and appreciation."

stories.headline: A global experiment: Can ESPN predict the Ballon d'Or awards?
stories.summary: The Ballon d'Or awards are typically tough to predict, but can ESPN and our global resources do just that?
stories.body:
The destination of the Ballon d'Or is typically tough to predict. Just ask Real Madrid's Vinícius Júnior, who, in 2024, had spent weeks believing he would win the men's award only to learn hours ahead of the ceremony that it had gone to Manchester City midfielder Rodri instead.

This year, it is no less straightforward.

On the men's side, there are plenty of candidates: Teenager Lamine Yamal dazzled for Barcelona, Harry Kane scored more goals for Bayern Munich than he ever has before, Kylian Mbappé starred for Real Madrid, while the 2026 World Cup saw Lionel Messi and Rodri compete to be named the competition's best player (in the end, it went to Rodri).

And for the Ballon d'Or Féminin, Alexia Putellas is the favorite after captaining Barcelona to another quadruple, but she was far from the only world-class player on that team.

The winners for both will be revealed on Oct. 26 at a glitzy ceremony in London, alongside a number of other awards, but is there a way to gauge who will walk away with the prizes ahead of time?

The men's Ballon d'Or is decided by a group of 100 journalists, each from different countries, while the Ballon d'Or Feminin's voting roll is made up of 50 journalists from 50 different countries. We decided to replicate that voting with ESPN journalists stationed all over the world.

Here's how we did it:

Methodology:

ESPN has a global team of journalists in every corner of the globe. We asked 20 ESPN journalists from around the world -- one per country -- to submit a ballot.
We used the official Ballon d'Or shortlists.
We had each voter submit their top five for the Ballon d'Or and their top three for all other awards.
Like official awards, each first-place vote received 15 points, followed by 12 points for second, 10 points for third, eight points for fourth and six points for fifth.

So, in a global experiment, can ESPN predict the Ballon d'Or?

Jump to:

Ballon d'Or | Women's Ballon d'Or

Other awards

BALLON D'OR: PLAYERS WHO GOT 1ST-PLACE VOTES

Lamine Yamal, Barcelona, RW

What our voters said:

Josué Utrilla, ESPN Guatemala reporter: "I believe that being a world champion -- while playing a key role in Spain's attack and enjoying excellent form with Barcelona in LaLiga -- demonstrates the talent he possesses at such a young age (19) and has earned him a place among football's biggest stars."

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich, ST

What our voters said:
Tom Hamilton, ESPN UK senior writer: "Okay, he didn't win the World Cup, or the Champions League, but Kane's year is unsurpassed. He scored 73 goals in 65 matches across the England national team and Bayern. It's a freakish record, the like of which we'll never see again. Let's park sentimentality and aesthetic-influenced bias; this award rewards individual brilliance."

Thijs Zwagerman, ESPN NL reporter: "Despite scoring goals at an extraordinary rate for years, Kane still does not receive the full recognition he deserves on the international stage. His qualities extend far beyond his remarkable goal-scoring record. He possesses the rare ability for a striker to drop deep, influence the game from a deeper position and operate like a playmaker as well. While Kane has yet to win the Champions League or the World Cup, that does not diminish his individual brilliance. In my view, he was still the best player in the world on an individual level."

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami CF, FW

What our voters said:
Anirudh Menon, ESPN India editor: "If this award is to be given to the best footballer on the planet, there can only be one answer. He may be 39 years old; he may even be playing in Major League Soccer (where he did win the MLS Cup and topped almost every attacking chart in the league), but the 2026 World Cup showed just how vast the gulf between Messi and everyone else remains. When he turns it on, there isn't anyone close. Give him his ninth Ballon d'Or already."

Teo Coquet, ESPN Argentina reporter: "I choose him because of his attacking influence and ability to remain decisive on the international stage. His performance for Argentina at the World Cup is also a key factor in my evaluation. At 39 years old, he has played one of the best World Cups of his career."

Kylian Mbappé, Real Madrid, ST

What our voters said:

Omar Flores, ESPN Mexico reporter: "Mbappé was the leading scorer across every competition he played in during the 2025-26 season, topping the charts in both the UEFA Champions League and Spain's LaLiga. At the World Cup, the France star scored 10 goals and became the tournament's all-time leading scorer (22 goals). Although he was unable to help his team advance beyond the semifinals, he remains one of the leading candidates to win the Ballon d'Or. "

Carlos Valdez, ESPN Colombia reporter: "I would put Mbappé first because of his extraordinary ability to make the difference at the highest level. His pace, finishing, consistency and capacity to deliver in decisive moments make him one of the most influential players in world football. His goal-scoring achievements across the league, Champions League and World Cup further strengthen his case. For me, the Ballon d'Or should recognize not only outstanding numbers, but also a player's ability to change the course of a game, and Mbappé embodies that quality."

Fabián Ruiz, Paris Saint-Germain, CM

What our voters said:

Moises Llorens, ESPN Spain reporter: "If we forget about the cameras, the spotlights, the commercial interests, and all the pomp that increasingly accompanies the business of football, then Ruiz should win the Ballon d'Or. I have no doubt about it. Why? It's simple. He was an undisputed and fundamental player for PSG's repeated Champions League title success last season, and was equally fundamental for Luis de la Fuente's victorious Spain side at the 2026 World Cup when Pedri wasn't at his best in midfield. Ruiz won it all over the past 12 months and was a standout player. He lacks marketing appeal, which will work against him, but he would be a deserving winner."

Rodri, Barcelona, CM

What our voters said:

Jean Beausejour, ESPN Chile analyst: "In a World Cup year, winning the tournament carries enormous weight. Rodri had a tremendous influence on Spain's performances on football's biggest stage. Spain's ability to dominate matches, control the tempo and impose their style of play against different opponents was largely down to Rodri's intelligence, positioning and exceptional ability to dictate the game. His influence went far beyond individual statistics, making him, in my opinion, the most deserving candidate for the Ballon d'Or."

ESPN'S PREDICTED WINNER: HARRY KANE

In a symbol of how divisive the men's Ballon d'Or race is, Kane received half of the first-place votes but only one of the other 10 voters put him second. Perhaps the biggest surprise was the large snubbing of Yamal, who received just a single No. 1 vote.

This was a two-horse race and, as ESPN writer Bill Connelly wrote earlier this month: "Kane played eight more matches and over 600 more minutes than Yamal -- which is to say, he stayed healthier than a player 14 years his junior -- and he produced 81 combined goals and assists, a full 36 more than Yamal."

There is a slice of history on offer for Kane, too: Kane would be just the fifth Englishman to cradle the golden trophy, alongside Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen.

BALLON D'OR FEMININE: PLAYERS WHO GOT 1ST-PLACE VOTES
Alexia Putellas, London City Lionesses, AM

What our voters said:

Leonard Solms, ESPN Africa reporter: "In her final season at Barcelona, midfield maestro Putellas not only captained Barcelona to the Liga F, UEFA Women's Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de España trophies -- but also scored 20 goals and assisted 14 in 43 games. Capable of filling multiple roles in the team, Putellas is the kind of player any manager would love to have 11 of, and her brilliance should not be taken for granted."

Marissa Lordanic, ESPN Australia editor: "Putellas was once again invaluable across multiple competitions. The epitome of a big-game player, she ensured Barcelona's trophy case continued to grow before she tested herself in a new league."

Ewa Pajor, Barcelona, ST

What our voters said:

Gustavo Hofman, ESPN Brasil reporter: "Pajor combined outstanding individual production with collective success and delivered when it mattered most. She recorded 34 goals and eight assists in 46 appearances for club and country, helping Barcelona win the Champions League, Liga F, Copa de la Reina and Spanish Super Cup. Her intelligent movement and clinical finishing gave Barcelona a cutting edge throughout the season, but her Champions League performances ultimately put her ahead of the competition: she finished as the tournament's top scorer with 11 goals and scored twice in the 4-0 victory over OL Lyonnes in the final."

Ed Dove, ESPN Africa reporter: "In recent years, Pajor's performances haven't always been rewarded with the silverware and honors one might expect. That changed last term, where she was a key influence -- and a major goal threat -- in Barcelona's historic Quadruple-winning campaign. A genuine big-game player, she scored 33 across all competitions, including 11 in the Champions League, where she struck in every knockout round Barca played in before netting twice in a one-sided final victory over OL Lyonnes. Pajor may have scored fewer than she did during his remarkable debut season at Barca, but after overcoming the UWCL final defeat by Arsenal in 2025, she deserves the individual recognition here."

Temwa Chawinga, Kansas City Current, FW

What our voters said:

Jeff Kassouf, ESPN (US) reporter: "No player changes a game like Chawinga. She can create chances on her own in one-vs.-one situations from literally inside her own half on the counter attack, and is a sharp goal scorer. Scoring 20 goals in the NWSL and then following that up with 15 the next season is dominant form at a world-class level. And she does it for club and country, having helped lowly Malawi to the 2027 World Cup. This time next year, more international opponents will know the fear of having Chawinga run at their defense."

Patri Guijarro, Barcelona, CM

What our voters said:

Moises Llorens, ESPN Spain: "The backbone of Barcelona's women's team and an excellent midfielder who makes runs from the second line. Other players usually steal the spotlight, but her talent is unquestionable. She makes the rest of the team shine."

ESPN'S PREDICTED WINNER: ALEXIA PUTELLAS
This result is not a surprise. Putellas is the clear favourite for the award, and our voters agreed.

Putellas enjoyed a dream end to her 14-year Barcelona career last season, captaining the club to a second Quadruple in three years, including lifting the Women's Champions League, before she moved to captain London City Lionesses, who are now third in the Women's Super League after five games.

Should Putellas actually win, she would earn her third Ballon d'Or award, joining former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmatí as its most frequent recipient.

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Previewing Bruins-Stars, all 10 other matchups on Tuesday
stories.summary: Twenty-two teams will be in action this evening. Here's what you need to know.
stories.body:
October is arguably the best month of the year for sports fans, and the NHL is doing its part Tuesday to create another special evening.

No, it's not the 16-game slate of the Frozen Frenzy, but there are 11 games on the calendar, including a number of tantalizing matchups between interconference contenders.

Here's a look at what you need to know for each contest, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

San Jose Sharks at Montreal Canadiens

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MTL -205, O/U: 6.5

After a visit to the Maple Leafs on Monday, Macklin Celebrini & Co. head to la Belle Province for a showdown against an as yet underperforming Canadiens team. Celebrini has had quite a bit of success against the Habs, with four goals and five assists in four games against Montreal in his career -- seven of those nine points came in the two matchups in 2025-26.

Colorado Avalanche at New Jersey Devils

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -115, O/U: 6.5

The Avalanche and Devils have faced off 102 times in the regular season in their history -- and once in a Stanley Cup Final that was historic for its intensity as well as Ray Bourque finally winning a title.

Back to current events, any game against a top team like this is a good barometer for a Devils club that is still figuring out what this season is going to look like. And on the other side, whichever member of the Lumber Yard is in the crease, it'll be familiar territory as both are ex-Devils.

Anaheim Ducks at New York Islanders

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYI -166, O/U: 6.5

Just 24 hours after facing off against the Rangers at Madison Square Garden, the Ducks will take to the ice at UBS Arena on Long Island before a date with the Devils on Thursday and finishing out their trip in Philadelphia on Saturday.

Specific to this game, it's a showdown between two of the top rookies from last season: Islanders defenseman Matthew Schaefer, who unanimously won the Calder Trophy, and Ducks winger Beckett Sennecke, who finished a point ahead of him in the rookie scoring race.

Los Angeles Kings at Washington Capitals

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WSH -166, O/U: 5.5

The Kings -- a playoff team last season -- are still on the hunt for their first win of the season. Will it be Tuesday? Of note, L.A. lost both games against the Capitals last season (2-1 on Nov. 17 and 3-1 on Dec. 2).

Washington brings a two-game winning streak into this matchup. The Caps are getting contributions from all over, but two offseason additions are leading the goal-scoring charge: Alex Tuch (five goals) and Boone Jenner (four).

Toronto Maple Leafs at Columbus Blue Jackets

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CBJ -162, O/U: 6.5

These teams made major news on the eve of opening night when they consummated a trade sending Kirill Marchenko to Toronto and Matthew Knies to Columbus (among six players moved in the swap).

Thus far, Marchenko has been the more lucrative player on the score sheet with nine points in nine games compared to four in seven for Knies. How do they each respond in this game -- and how do the Columbus fans welcome back Marchenko, who signaled an unwillingness to re-sign with the Blue Jackets, which led to the trade?

Winnipeg Jets at St. Louis Blues

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | STL -142, O/U: 5.5

Any game between Central Division foes is a must-watch, but the added wrinkle in any Jets game this fall is the Connor Hellebuyck saga. The latest, per ESPN's Emily Kaplan, is that there are three teams in the mix to trade for the former Hart and Vezina Trophy winner.

Though all of the off-ice business was generating buzz on message boards, the Jets are off to a 4-2-2 start, three points ahead of the Blues heading into this showdown. A key for the Blues? Scoring more than two goals. They've lost all four games in which they've scored two or fewer, and won three of the four in which they've scored more than two goals.

Boston Bruins at Dallas Stars

8 p.m. ET (ESPN) | DAL -170, O/U: 5.5

And speaking of U.S. Olympic goaltenders, this contest could feature a showdown between Boston's Jeremy Swayman and Dallas' Jake Oettinger. According to ESPN Research, Oettinger (187) and Swayman (138) and second and third, respectively, for the most wins by an American goalie since 2020-21 (behind Hellebuyck's 197).

On the goal-scoring side, there will be superstars on both sides as David Pastrnak (No. 8), Mikko Rantanen (15) and Jason Robertson (20) all landed in the top 20 of ESPN's annual player rankings.

Minnesota Wild at Edmonton Oilers

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | EDM -130, O/U: 6.5

This matchup has even more star power, with Connor McDavid (No. 1), Leon Draisaitl (6), Quinn Hughes (9) and Kirill Kaprizov (10) all in the top 10. It would be a shocking outcome if either of these teams missed the playoffs, and Stathletes projects a 6.36% chance of the pair squaring off in the Western Conference finals this spring; that's the fifth-highest percentage of any WCF pairing.

The Wild won all three games in the season series in 2025-26 by a combined score of 13-5. How will Game 1 of the 2026-27 series go?

Detroit Red Wings at Seattle Kraken

9:40 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SEA -118, O/U: 6.5

It has been an up-and-down season for the Red Wings, following one of the more chaotic offseasons for any team in recent memory. But, they're on a two-game win streak so maybe things are turning around?

Standing in their way of continuing that heater are the Kraken, who produced a 6-3 win over the Red Wings on Oct. 9. And don't look now, but the Kraken might be a real contender in the Pacific, holding down the No. 3 spot as we close in on a month into the campaign.

Carolina Hurricanes at Vancouver Canucks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CAR -278, O/U: 6.5

Some might look at that large number on the betting line and conclude that this game might be a blowout for the visiting Cup champs. Well, the Canes were -218 against the Flames on Sunday, and lost that one. So anything is possible.

If the Canucks are to present a real challenge Tuesday, they'll need to get back to their early high-scoring ways. After netting 17 goals in their first three games, they've scored 13 in the next seven.

Tampa Bay Lightning at Vegas Golden Knights

10:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | VGK -112, O/U: 5.5

In the marquee matchup of the night, it's a potential Stanley Cup Final preview -- and in fact, Stathletes projects a 3.67% chance of this being the SCF matchup (which is third highest). The Lightning won the Cup in 2020 and 2021, and the Golden Knights won in 2023, and made the Cup Final in 2026.

The superstars will be out in this matchup. Jack Eichel (18 points through 10 games) and Mark Stone (14 through 10) are both scoring above career-best paces. Tampa's Nikita Kucherov (10 through eight) is off his usual pace near the league lead, but maybe he's due for a big night: his 1.86 points-per-game rate against Vegas is the highest of anyone against the franchise.

stories.headline: Animal rights group PETA call for Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot
stories.summary: Animal rights group PETA has urged Crystal Palace to retire the club's bald eagle mascot, Phoenix, with immediate effect.
stories.body:
Animal rights group PETA has urged Crystal Palace to retire the club's bald eagle mascot, Phoenix, with immediate effect.

In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, PETA has demanded the club commit to "never using a live animal mascot again."

Palace's previous eagle mascot, Kayla, regularly appeared before matches at Selhurst Park and flew the length of the pitch.

But PETA says that "reclusive eagles deserve better than a stressful, booming stadium environment" where "bright lights, loud noises, and boisterous crowds can cause birds to become frightened, disoriented and panicked."

The letter cited other incidents involving live birds at football including "an owl who died after being hit by a ball, eagles who crashed into walls or glass windows, and a falcon who landed on a fan's head, sinking his talons into the man's scalp."

"In another case," Peta continued, "a rowdy football supporter punched a rival team's eagle mascot."

That incident is believed to relate to a fan attacking Kayla at a League Cup match against south London rivals Charlton, which was marred by crowd trouble, in September 2015.

"Bald eagles are revered as symbols of freedom, yet Phoenix is being used as little more than a prop to entertain football fans," PETA's Dr Carys Bennett said.

"Crystal Palace already has a human mascot to energise supporters, so there's no reason to drag a wild animal into a noisy, crowded stadium.

"PETA is urging the club to let Phoenix spread his wings and retire him from matchday duties for good."

Palace, whose nickname has been the Eagles since 1973, have been contacted for comment.

stories.headline: Lisandro Martínez, Marcus Rashford miss Man United training ahead of Como clash
stories.summary: Lisandro Martínez and Marcus Rashford missed training ahead of the trip to Como as Manchester United's injury problems continued to mount.
stories.body:
Lisandro Martínez and Marcus Rashford missed training ahead of the trip to Como as Manchester United's injury problems continued to mount.

Martínez's eventful week, which saw him apologise after publicly criticising the club's hierarchy, ended with him keeping his place for Sunday's Premier League clash against Leeds only to be forced off with a thigh complaint.

Rashford was an unused substitute at Elland Road and United confirmed on Tuesday that he is "managing an injury issue."

The England forward and Martínez were among eight players who missed training at Carrington along with Ayden Heaven, Luke Shaw, Kobbie Mainoo, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Manuel Ugarte.

Shaw and Mainoo have both missed the last two matches, Heaven was absent from the Leeds game through illness, while Sesko, Dorgu and Ugarte are all injured.

Meanwhile, Matthijs de Ligt is back in training but has not yet featured following back surgery while fellow defender Lenny Yoro is suspended for the Champions League clash in Italy.
